plan.angle: Lane A (log 'lane: A'), 'Life on Tirzepatide' series, 8–12 min, 14:00 ET, evergreen, no news peg. The first spoken sentence answers the title with a 'you' scenario: 'Your first Thanksgiving on tirzepatide can feel different: you may fill up faster, and big, rich meals may sit heavier. A little planning, mostly around protein, portion size and pace, helps you enjoy it.' Chapters named as searched questions: (1) Why does a big meal feel different on tirzepatide? Credit only the FDA label wording (it can delay gastric emptying; GI side effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are common). (2) What should I put on my plate? Build it around turkey or another protein you enjoy, then whatever else you like. Credit only what the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory (Mozaffarian et al., Obesity 2025, PMC12304835) says: getting enough protein, and that 'avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment' can ease nausea. Quote that exact scope and don't stretch it to holidays. Smaller plates, starting with a small serving and going back if you're still hungry, and leftovers boxes are our own tips with no source tag. (3) How fast should I eat? Eating slowly and stopping when comfortably full are our own tips, untagged. (4) What about drinks? Sip fluids through the day unless you've been told to limit fluids. The label warns that vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration. For alcohol, make no sourced claim: ask your prescriber. If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, the label notes a higher risk of low blood sugar, so ask your prescriber about the holiday. (5) What if I feel too full or queasy? Common comfort steps, plus the label's warning signs (severe stomach pain that won't go away) and 'contact your healthcare provider'. (6) Leftovers, the next day and movement: an optional walk after the meal is our own tip; the advisory's strength-training point stays at its exact wording. (7) Mindset: no guilt, no foods labelled 'bad', no calorie talk, no 'earning' food, and enjoying the people as much as the plate. Anyone with a history of disordered eating should follow their care team's plan. Explicitly say: don't skip, move or change your injection or dose around the holiday on your own; that's a conversation with your prescriber. Never mention dose numbers. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the plate payoff. Include 'Not personal advice', 'don't stop or change your medicines on your own' and the full prescriber line. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' No spoken titles and never 'on screen'. Thumbnail: 4 words or fewer, a warm reaction layout with one labelled character at a holiday table (e.g. 'Full Already?'). Sources: the joint advisory and the FDA Zepbound/Mounjaro label only. Drop the YouGov hook unless a primary URL can be opened.

package.description:
Quick answer: the FDA labels say tirzepatide delays gastric emptying, so a big holiday meal may sit heavier and you may fill up faster. Nausea is one of the most common side effects. One priority in a 2025 joint advisory on nutrition with GLP-1 medicines for obesity: get enough protein.

Not personal advice. Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine. Don't skip, move or change your injection or dose, and don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
Zepbound Prescribing Information (FDA): https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/217806s000lbl.pdf
Mounjaro Prescribing Information (FDA): https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/215866s000lbl.pdf
Joint GLP-1 nutrition advisory, Obesity 2025: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/

scenes.section: Your first Thanksgiving on tirzepatide
scenes.narration: Quick note first. This is general information, not personal advice. Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you, and about your own holiday plan.

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: So, first question. Why does a big meal feel so different on tirzepatide?

visual.stock_query: curious stomach character at dinner table

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: The answer is in the official prescribing information for Zepbound and Mounjaro. Both FDA labels say tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. In plain English, food leaves your stomach more slowly.

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: Think of your stomach like a sink with the drain partly closed. Pour in a holiday-sized meal, and it fills up faster than you expect.

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: Here's a detail most people never hear. The Mounjaro label says this delay is largest after the first dose, and the effect diminishes over time.

visual.stock_query: calendar pages turning with calm stomach

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: So the way your stomach feels in your first weeks may not be how it feels months later, though stomach side effects can be more common when the dose is increased. Everyone's experience is a little different.

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: The labels also list stomach symptoms among the most common side effects: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, stomach pain and indigestion.

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: Now picture those facts next to a classic holiday table. Big portions, rich gravy, buttery sides, two kinds of pie, and hours of grazing.
scenes.retention_device: Collision of facts and familiar scene

scenes.section: Why does a big meal feel different?
scenes.narration: You can see why it might sit heavier. But here's the good news: the answer isn't skipping everything you love. It starts with what lands on your plate first.
scenes.retention_device: But/therefore re-hook into the next chapter

scenes.narration: So, what should you actually put on your plate?

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: Start with turkey, or another protein you enjoy. Ham, salmon, tofu, beans, whatever your table has. Then add whatever else you love.

visual.stock_query: turkey slices placed first on plate

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: Why protein? In twenty twenty-five, four major lifestyle medicine, nutrition and obesity organizations published a joint advisory on nutrition for people using GLP-1 medicines for obesity.

visual.stat_label: organizations behind the 2025 joint nutrition advisory

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: One of its clear priorities: getting enough protein.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: Putting it on first is our own idea, not the advisory's. When your appetite is smaller, your plate has less room. Protein first means it doesn't get crowded out by the bread basket.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't let it get crowded out

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: Back to Dana. She used to pile on everything at once. This year, she starts with a few slices of turkey, then picks the two sides she's waited all year for.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: Notice what's missing: a forbidden list. The stuffing is allowed. The pie is allowed. This is about order and portion, not rules.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: But wait. What about the rich stuff? You may have heard that fatty foods are off-limits on tirzepatide. That's not quite what the advisory says.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: Its tip is narrower. It says that avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can ease nausea.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: That scope matters: the first few days of treatment. It isn't a holiday rule. But if Thanksgiving falls in your very first days on the medicine, it's worth asking your prescriber about.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: A few more ideas, and these are simply ours. Try a smaller plate. Start with a small serving of each favorite. If you're still hungry later, go back. The food isn't going anywhere.

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: And set out leftovers boxes from the start. Then 'I couldn't finish it' becomes 'I'm saving some for tomorrow.'

scenes.section: What should I put on my plate?
scenes.narration: So that's the plate plan. Protein first, favorites next, small servings, and a box for later.

scenes.narration: Now, the plate is only half the story. How fast you eat it may matter just as much.

scenes.narration: So, how fast should you eat?

scenes.section: How fast should I eat?
scenes.narration: Remember that slow-draining sink. Our take: when food leaves your stomach more slowly, it can be easy to overshoot before you notice you're full.

visual.stock_query: sink filling to the brim cartoon

scenes.section: How fast should I eat?
scenes.narration: These next tips are our own, not from a study. Eat slowly. Put your fork down between bites. Talk, laugh, pass the cranberry sauce.

scenes.section: How fast should I eat?
scenes.narration: Halfway through, check in. Ask yourself: am I comfortably full, or still hungry? Comfortably full is the goal, not stuffed.

scenes.section: How fast should I eat?
scenes.narration: Dana tries it. Halfway through, she stops to toast her sister. When she picks her fork back up, she realizes she's already satisfied. So she boxes the rest.

visual.stock_query: Dana toasting sister with water glass

scenes.section: How fast should I eat?
scenes.narration: And here's a lovely side effect of eating slowly: you get more of the thing you actually came for. The people.

scenes.section: How fast should I eat?
scenes.narration: But food isn't the only thing on the table. That glass next to your plate deserves its own plan too.

scenes.section: What about drinks?
scenes.narration: Start with the simple one. Sipping water through the day is an easy habit, unless your care team has told you to limit fluids.

scenes.section: What about drinks?
scenes.narration: Here's why fluids matter. The Zepbound label warns that diarrhea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids, called dehydration.

scenes.section: What about drinks?
scenes.narration: Small, steady sips also tend to feel easier on a full stomach than gulping a big glass at once. That one's our tip, not the label's.

scenes.section: What about drinks?
scenes.narration: What about alcohol? We're not giving you a rule here. That's a question for your prescriber, who knows your health and your other medicines.

scenes.section: What about drinks?
scenes.narration: One more point, and it's an important one. If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea for diabetes, the labels note a higher risk of low blood sugar when they're combined with tirzepatide.

scenes.section: What about drinks?

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: First, it happens, and it isn't a failure. One overfull afternoon is just one afternoon.

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: Some gentle comfort steps, again our own suggestions: stop eating, loosen your waistband, sit upright instead of lying flat, sip water slowly, and step outside for fresh air.

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: You might be tempted to skip or delay your injection to dodge the queasiness. Please don't skip, move or change your injection or dose around the holiday on your own.

visual.stock_query: person pausing with phone to call clinic

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: That's a conversation with your prescriber, ideally well before the big day. And don't stop or change your medicines on your own.

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: Now, the warning signs. The label lists severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, as a reason to call your healthcare provider right away.

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: That pain may also be felt from your stomach through to your back.

visual.stock_query: simple body outline with arrow to back

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: That's different from ordinary after-dinner fullness, which eases with time. If you're ever unsure, call. That's what they're there for.

scenes.section: What if I feel too full or queasy?
scenes.narration: Dana, by the way, felt comfortably full by four o'clock. But then came the question every host knows: what do I do with all these leftovers?

scenes.section: Leftovers, the next day and movement
scenes.narration: Leftovers are your friend. With a smaller appetite, one holiday meal can stretch into several easy, enjoyable meals.

scenes.section: Leftovers, the next day and movement
scenes.narration: The next day, there's nothing to make up for. No detox, no skipping meals to compensate. Just go back to your usual rhythm. And the joint advisory's priority still applies: get enough protein.

scenes.section: Leftovers, the next day and movement
scenes.narration: Movement can be part of the day too, gently. A relaxed walk after the meal is our own suggestion. It's a nice way to get some air and keep the conversation going.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe. I found one minor wording issue, and the fix is below.

What I checked against the sources:
- **Joint advisory (src1):** it exists in Obesity (Silver Spring), 2025, from the four organisations named. It calls for getting enough protein and for "regular strength training at least three times weekly". The s24 quote matches the printed words exactly: "avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms". The script keeps the advisory to that "first few days" scope and correctly marks protein-first, eating slowly, smaller plates, sips and walking as our own tips.
- **Mounjaro label (src3):** I confirmed the line "Tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. The delay is largest after the first dose and this effect diminishes over time."
- **Other label claims (src2, src3):** I couldn't get the text out of either FDA PDF; both URLs load, but the files came back as unreadable binary. These claims match the standard wording of both labels and their Medication Guides, so I didn't confirm them sentence by sentence:
  - the most common stomach side effects (s13);
  - fluid loss and dehydration from diarrhea, nausea and vomiting (s40);
  - higher risk of low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea (s43);
  - severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, possibly felt through to the back (s52–s53).

Safety:
- The script includes "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line (s07, s77), and the don't-stop/change line (s51, s76).
- It says not to skip or move a dose around the holiday (s50).
- It covers people told to limit fluids, people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, and people with a history of disordered eating.
- Alcohol is referred to the prescriber, and there's no restrictive-eating or detox messaging.

Hypothetical scenes: Dana and the aunt are clearly framed as imagined, not as real people.

The title is paid off in the first sentence, and the open loop (the sentence to say at the table) pays off in s65.

Source URLs: src2 and src3 point to the original 2022 and 2023 label versions. Those still exist, and the cited content carries over into the current labels.

issues.claim: stomach side effects can show up again after a dose change
issues.problem: The labels tie stomach side effects to dose escalation (increases). "A dose change" is broader than that, because it also covers decreases. The overstatement is small.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "So the way your stomach feels in your first weeks may not be how it feels months later, though stomach side effects can be more common when the dose is increased. Everyone's experience is a little different."

audio.soundNotes: Music under voice (-13.5dB) and in pauses (-15.8dB) already sit in the target window, so only a small +0.4dB nudge (gain 1.05) to bring pause swells a touch closer to -14dB; no further reduction needed. Pulled down a handful of cues that read hot over speech (swoosh/pop/hit at -6 to -10dB rel. voice near 27s, 203.75s, 220.5s, 467s and 585.4s) to the -14 to -16dB felt range, and zeroed out redundant blips/pops in the densest chip-reveal clusters (holiday game plan, stomach side effects/also common, our tips, plate plan, our suggestions, checklist chips) to keep each burst at 2-4 effects per second per the brief. Added five bespoke, quiet accent sounds for key emotional beats (Dana's intro, the insulin/sulfonylurea caution, warning-signs heartbeat, the "call" moment, and the cozy "nothing went to waste" payoff) to add warmth without ever approaching the voice.

issues: Subtext 'Your first holiday plate' is small and may be hard to read instantly at phone size
Face expression reads as a plain smile, not a strong 'surprised/full' emotion, weakening the hook
Two separate characters (plate face + turkey face) split focus instead of one clear hero, diluting the single emotional beat
Headline text is noticeably smaller/denser than the other two candidates, slightly harder to scan instantly

thumbnail.reasoning: All three stay within the 4-word headline rule and don't repeat the title. #2 ('WHY IT SITS HEAVIER') pairs a single, clearly labelled, emotionally expressive hero (the surprised stomach) with large bold legible text and strong blue/yellow contrast — it best matches the playbook's reaction-layout CTR edge (median ~6.1%) and the 'one labelled character, one honest emotion' rule, and it ties directly to chapter 1's mechanism hook without giving away the answer. #0 has a clean single character but the facial expression is too neutral to sell 'FULL ALREADY?', and its secondary line is small at phone size. #1 (before-after) has strong contrast and a clever visual payoff, but splits attention across two characters/faces and uses smaller type, which slightly undercuts the one-glance legibility and focal clarity the other two achieve. #2 wins on the combination of CTR pull and legibility.

issues.claim: A 2025 joint advisory's priority: get enough protein.
issues.problem: The script says protein is "one of its clear priorities". Calling it the advisory's priority makes it sound like the only one. The sentence also leaves out who the advisory covers (people using GLP-1 medicines for obesity).
issues.fix: Replace with: "One priority in a 2025 joint advisory on nutrition with GLP-1 medicines for obesity: get enough protein."

issues.claim: Chapters end at "8:47 How do I enjoy it without guilt?"
issues.problem: The script has a final section, "Your Thanksgiving checklist", but it has no chapter. Viewers can't jump to the checklist, which is the part most worth coming back to.
issues.fix: Add a final chapter line "[timestamp] Your Thanksgiving checklist", using the start time of the checklist section in the rendered video. If you can't get that timestamp, rename the last line to: "8:47 Enjoy it without guilt, plus your checklist".

issues.problem: The script hedges ("may sit heavier", "might sit heavier"), and the thumbnail drops the hedge. This is acceptable within the 4-word limit, and the video explains the reason, so the change is optional.
issues.fix: Optional: "WHY IT MAY FEEL HEAVIER" (5 words; keep the current text if the 4-word limit is strict).
